name: Compression binder / binding bra

card.summary: A tight compression garment that flattens the chest so clothing sits smoothly, used by transmasculine people and by men with gynecomastia.
card.note: Commonly reported effects include pain, breathing restriction and skin irritation; DIY materials carry more risk.

quick.overview:
A chest binder is a compression garment, often spandex or nylon, that flattens the chest. It gives a flatter silhouette under clothing, which is its appearance payoff.

It is used most by transgender men and non-binary people to ease dysphoria and create a masculine profile, and also by some cisgender men with gynecomastia. Research on binding is mostly surveys and small pilot studies.
quick.how: People wear a commercial binder or a compression top under clothes during the day. Community guidance referenced by Wikipedia advises correct sizing and not sleeping in one; DIY elastic bandages or tape are considered higher risk.
quick.risks: Surveys find most people who bind report some physical effects, including back pain, shortness of breath, overheating, chest pain, rashes and, rarely, rib fractures [1]. A 2025 pilot study examined exercise capacity with binding in adolescents [2], and a case report described oxygen desaturation [3]. Many binders still report psychological benefit [1].

lead: A compression binder, or binding bra, flattens the chest through firm elastic compression. Users wear it to change the chest's outline so shirts hang flat, a direct visual effect [1].

Chest binding has a long history, from Chinese moxiong and dudou and Japanese sarashi to Victorian corsets and 1920s flapper fashion [1]. Today it is used mostly by transmasculine and non-binary people, and by some cisgender men with gynecomastia [1].

Research is mainly cross-sectional surveys and pilot work: a 2024 community-informed survey compared commercial and non-commercial binders [4], and a 2025 pilot study looked at exercise testing in gender diverse youth who bind [2].

angle.text: The garment visibly flattens the chest under clothes. It is worn temporarily and the effect ends when it is removed.

paras: Commercial binders are purpose-built garments, while others use sports bras, layered tops or specialist tape; elastic bandages, duct tape and plastic wrap are DIY materials associated with the highest risk [1].

Wikipedia summarises that almost everyone who binds notes some physical effect, such as back pain, breathlessness, overheating, chest or shoulder pain and skin irritation; rib fractures are rare [1]. A 2017 study found commercial binders among the riskier methods and sports bras among the least harmful [1]. A 2024 survey linked binding to lower anxiety and dysphoria in respondents [1].
Community posts reported in 2026 that the US FDA sent warning letters to companies selling binders, alleging misbranded medical devices [5].

A 2025 pilot study tested whether binding affected cardiopulmonary exercise testing and spirometry in transgender and gender diverse youth assigned female at birth [2]. A 2022 case report described prolonged oxygen desaturation in a transgender man who bound [3]. A 2024 cross-sectional survey examined physical and mental changes among users of commercial and non-commercial binders [4].
